title: Chop-and-drop mulching
subtitle: Cutting back plants and leaving them on the soil surface to decompose in place.
excerpt: Chop and drop is the practice of cutting back herbaceous plants and leaving all the cut material on the bed surface as mulch. It requires no compost bin, no carrying, and no turning. The cut material breaks down on the soil surface and feeds the plants growing below.
sourceNotes: Technique from David Holmgren, Permaculture: Principles and Pathways Beyond Sustainability (2002). Application to comfrey and dynamic accumulators in Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Breakdown rates from general organic horticulture literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cutting a plant (usually a dynamic accumulator or cover crop) and leaving all the material on the soil surface rather than removing it. The cut material acts as a mulch, suppressing weeds and decomposing to feed soil organisms. It is the simplest possible way to return nutrients to the soil without a compost heap.

content.text: is the simplest fertility management method in a permaculture garden. Cut back comfrey, nettles, or any herbaceous plant, and lay the cut material flat on the soil surface. Worms process it from below; sun and rain break it down from above. Within two to four weeks in summer, little remains.
Best plants for chop and drop

Comfrey is the classic chop-and-drop plant: high in potassium and fast to break down. Nettles are high in nitrogen. Phacelia and buckwheat (cut before seed set) work well in summer gaps. Grass clippings are useful in thin layers but form a mat if applied too thickly.

Cut the plant to the ground with shears or a scythe. Lay the cut material in a layer 3 to 5 cm thick across the bed surface or around the base of fruit trees and shrubs. Spread it evenly: a thick mat takes longer to break down and can host slugs. Avoid cutting the same plant more than three times in a season.

attrs.title: Chop and drop under fruit trees
attrs.body: Comfrey planted in a ring around a fruit tree and cut three to four times a year provides a steady flow of nutrients to the tree's root zone. Cut the comfrey and leave it under the tree. It breaks down quickly in warm weather and the potassium it contains is exactly what fruiting trees need. There is no need to water it in or incorporate it.
